blindConstruct: Identify the standardized 4-letter scale abbreviation used to quantify opioid-withdrawal severity before medication dosing
blindUniqueness: MODERATE — SOWS and OOWS are also legitimate 4-letter opioid-withdrawal scales; COWS is correct for objective bedside scoring used in buprenorphine/methadone initiation protocols but competing abbreviations exist
reason: COWS (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale) is the standard objective bedside tool used in medication-dosing protocols; the stem's enumerated withdrawal signs (HR 104, dilated pupils, rhinorrhea, yawning, piloerection, cramping, anxiety) anchor the clinical picture unambiguously to opioid withdrawal, and the 4-letter constraint is a scaffold not a giveaway. Recall of COWS is a legitimate NCLEX-level nursing knowledge point tied directly to clinical workflow and medication-initiation thresholds, not purely definitional vocabulary. Uniqueness is moderate because SOWS and OOWS share the same letter count; a scoring rubric should key COWS and flag SOWS/OOWS for clinical adjudication rather than auto-reject.

blindConstruct: Differentiate SIADH from CSWS and other causes of hyponatremia using the complete post-SAH discriminating dataset (hypo-osmolar plasma, concentrated urine, natriuresis, euvolemia, exclusion of adrenal/thyroid/renal/glucose causes)
blindUniqueness: HIGH — serum Na 122 + serum osm 260 + urine osm 520 + urine Na 58 + euvolemia (normal BP, moist mucous membranes, no edema) + post-SAH context + exclusion of all other causes converges uniquely on SIADH; CSWS is the only real differential and is excluded by euvolemia markers
reason: High-quality diagnostic-reasoning item. SIADH vs CSWS is the canonical post-SAH clinical dilemma; the treatments are opposite (fluid restriction vs fluid resuscitation), so correct identification has direct management consequence. The stem provides a fully discriminating dataset: euvolemia (normal BP, moist membranes, no edema) excludes CSWS which produces hypovolemia, while the lab pattern (urine osm > serum osm, high urine Na, hyponatremia) with systematic exclusion of adrenal/thyroid/renal/glucose causes closes the differential to SIADH. The acronym-recall format is appropriate because SIADH names a specific, well-defined clinical syndrome with a standard management algorithm.

blindConstruct: Sequence nursing interventions for life-threatening hyperkalemia (K+ 7.1, widened QRS) in ESKD with functioning dialysis access: establish cardiac monitoring → cardiac-membrane stabilization → cellular redistribution → definitive potassium removal → post-treatment reassessment
blindUniqueness: HIGH — each position is anchored by a distinct physiologic rationale; the widened-QRS finding makes cardiac stabilization (B) unambiguously prior to redistribution (C); only arguable swap is B↔C which is weak given the cardiac-toxicity signal
reason: The ordered-response construct is clinically grounded and non-arbitrary. Step rationale: (A) cardiac monitoring establishes baseline rhythm before any intervention — universal prerequisite; (B) IV calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac membrane immediately — widened QRS signals imminent arrhythmia risk and calcium acts within minutes without lowering K+; (C) insulin+dextrose shifts K+ intracellularly over 15-30 min, bridging to definitive treatment; (D) urgent hemodialysis is the only intervention that actually removes potassium from the body and is the definitive step; (E) post-treatment recheck of K+, glucose, and rhythm closes the safety loop. The sole competing arrangement (C before B) is refuted by the widened-QRS finding which makes cardiac protection the immediate priority over redistribution. defensibleOrderCount = 1 for exam purposes.
